sections.h2: Ways to sell a Peekskill house
sections.html:
Selling in Peekskill can mean a broker listing, a for-sale-by-owner deal, or a straight cash purchase. Whatever the route, city paperwork decides your timetable. The city is in northwestern Westchester County, 35 miles up the Hudson from Manhattan, which draws buyers from more than one direction.

Paying cash skips a mortgage appraisal and lender review. The deed, transfer forms and taxes still apply. Sellers here are most often surprised by two things: the Certificate of Occupancy that a lender requests, and a city transfer tax stacked on the state's.

The city counted 25,431 people in 2020 and an estimated 25,891 on July 1, 2025. Only 59.4 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, which leaves a big rental market. Owned homes have a median value of $395,600. Rent runs a median of $2,036 monthly, household income has a median of $85,954 across 10,777 households, and the typical commute is 37.2 minutes.

Rents that high and trips that long point to commuters and working renters. A landlord selling an occupied building should have the leases ready, plus proof that each unit is legal.

Peekskill has a Metro-North station with trains to New York City, 41 miles south, plus Bee-Line bus routes. A house near the station appeals to commuters, so state the walking distance in your listing. The whole city is in a single district, the Peekskill City School District.

Think of the department as the office that vouches for your permit file. It handles permits for buildings, driveways, fences and signs. It also issues the Certificate of Compliance or Occupancy that finishes a permit or backs up a home sale. A lender wants the Certificate of Occupancy along with the mortgage application, which means a buyer relying on a loan may be held up if yours is missing.

Permits are required for additions, expansions, conversions, major alterations, garages, decks, finished basements and pools. The city also actively seeks out illegal apartments and pushes substandard property toward code. Built a kitchen, deck or rental unit with no paperwork? Call 914-734-4140 before you list.

  • Visits to the office need an appointment. Send applications by mail or leave them in the drop boxes at City Hall, 840 Main Street. Processing takes up to two weeks.
  • With no open permits, violations or complaints, an inspector may accept a virtual walk-through for the Certificate of Occupancy.
  • An open permit, violation or complaint means an in-person inspection, as does any commercial or multi-family building.

sections.h2: Transfer taxes for a Peekskill seller
sections.html:
A Peekskill seller pays twice over. The state collects $2 on each $500 of price, and at $1 million or more the buyer owes an extra 1 percent mansion tax. The state return, Form TP-584, goes to the county clerk, with a 15 day limit after the deed is delivered.

The city layers on a tax of its own under Local Law 11 of 2010: 1 percent of the sale price. The seller owes it within 30 days after handing over the deed, before the deed is recorded. On every deed, taxable or not, buyer and seller sign a single return for the city Comptroller. File late and you pay an 8 percent penalty plus interest each month. Get the current form from the Finance Department before closing.

sections.h2: Where a Peekskill deed is recorded
sections.html:
Recording happens at the Land Records Division of the Westchester County Clerk. You build the filing online in the clerk's PREP system, which asks for a cover page, the TP-584, the RP-5217 transfer report and a payment page. The clerk takes the state tax at filing and rounds the price up to the next $500.

Expect a $45 recording fee, $5 for each written side, $5 to file the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 when the property is a residence ($250 otherwise). Call (914) 995-3094 with questions. Clerk's staff cannot write your deed, so an attorney has to.

Values come from the City Assessor, who sends no bills. Ask the Finance Department, at 914-734-4109, for amounts and due dates. Assessment dates run like this:

  • May 1 is the valuation date, the taxable status date and the last day to file exemption forms.
  • June 1 brings the tentative roll.
  • Third Tuesday of June: Grievance Day, listed as June 15 for 2027.
  • New STAR filers apply to the state; the city does not accept those forms.

To dispute a value, pull recent nearby sales from the assessor's sales data and file before Grievance Day.

Closing goes faster when the open items are already cleared. Order a certified copy of your deed from the Westchester County Clerk and read it for names and signing requirements. Find out from the Building Department whether a Certificate of Occupancy is on file. Ask the Finance Department for any balance owed to the city, and for the city transfer tax form so it is ready to sign at the table. Then choose an attorney, who will prepare the deed, the TP-584 and the RP-5217.

If tenants live in the house, give the buyer copies of every lease early. Buyers financing with a loan also need time for the appraisal, so a cash buyer can often set a firmer date. Whoever you sell to, ask for the offer in writing and have your attorney review the contract before you sign it. Keep copies of everything you file, since the city and the county each keep separate records of the same sale.

Settle title and permits before you decide how to sell. Start here:

  • Get a certified deed copy from the Westchester clerk and confirm who has to sign.
  • Ask the Building Department if a Certificate of Occupancy is on file and any permit remains open.
  • Ask Finance about back city taxes and the 1 percent filing.
  • Collect leases for every occupied unit.
  • Weigh an as-is cash offer against broker fees and repair time.

An estate may need court paperwork before anyone is allowed to convey. A probate attorney can say who holds signing authority, and the title company will want that answered before it schedules a closing.

faqs.q: How fast can a Peekskill house close?
faqs.a: Faster with cash, since no lender is involved, and slower when a mortgage buyer needs an appraisal. City steps add time too, because Building Department applications take up to two weeks.

faqs.q: Is there a separate city tax on Peekskill sales?
faqs.a: Yes. Peekskill's Local Law 11 of 2010 sets 1 percent of the price, paid by the seller before recording, in addition to the state's $2 per $500.

faqs.q: Is a Certificate of Occupancy required to close in Peekskill?
faqs.a: Lenders ask for one on financed purchases, and the Building Department issues it. A house with open permits, violations or unpermitted work will likely need an inspection first, so call 914-734-4140 before you list.

faqs.q: Which day is Peekskill's Grievance Day?
faqs.a: The third Tuesday in June, listed as June 15 for 2027. The tentative roll comes out June 1 and exemption forms are due May 1.

faqs.q: Who records deeds for Peekskill properties?
faqs.a: The Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division, with a PREP cover page, the TP-584, the RP-5217 and payment of the fees and state tax.
